Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Romania's National Health Insurance House (CNAS) will launch its new e-Sănătatea Mea (My e-Health) platform on September 1, giving patients direct access to their digital health records and healthcare information for the first time. The platform is expected to serve nearly 20 million potential users through a single online interface. CNAS presented the platform's main functionalities during a debate organised by the Bucharest Center for Economy & Society (CES Bucharest) on Thursday, July 30. According to the institution, users will be able to access a personal digital health wallet containing their consultation history, diagnostic investigations, hospital admissions, reimbursed prescriptions, digital medical documents, health insurance status, and information on healthcare services reimbursed by CNAS. The platform will also allow patients to book appointments online with healthcare providers contracted by CNAS. Users will be able to authenticate through Romania's ROeID digital identity system or via a healthcare provider that has a contract with CNAS. “The e-Sănătatea Mea platform marks the most significant digital transformation in the relationship between patients and the healthcare system over the past 20 years," said Horațiu Moldovan, president of the National Health Insurance House, as quoted in a CES Bucharest press release. “From September 1, we are transitioning to a patient-centred system designed for nearly 20 million potential users. For the first time, every patient will have access, through a single interface, to their personal digital health wallet, where they will be able to book appointments online, review the history of their healthcare services and prescriptions, access digital medical forms, and verify their healthcare entitlements and the services reimbursed by CNAS," he added. According to CNAS, the platform has been designed to work alongside the software already used by hospitals and medical practices without requiring changes to their existing systems. Officials also said the platform could be expanded in the future with preventive healthcare features, including personalized reminders for medical check-ups, screening programmes, and recommended vaccinations. “The platform does not replace the existing methods of accessing healthcare services but complements them and will continue to be developed progressively, based on feedback received from patients and healthcare professionals,” reads the press release. irina.marica@romania-insider.com (Photo source: CES Bucharest) Read next 30 June 2026 Healthcare Romania had 72,000 healthcare facilities in 2025, 13,000 in rural areas Normal Healthcare Romania's national digital health platform to go live in a month 31 July 2026 Irina Marica Like this article? https://business-review.eu/business/86-o.text: 86% of Romanians believe air in their homes is cleaner than the air outside, even though their bodies tell them otherwise (study) We have grown accustomed to discomfort and stopped looking for its cause The study reveals a profound cognitive disconnect among the population: people have learned to normalize unpleasant physical symptoms and attribute them to stress or fatigue at work. Morning tiredness, even after eight hours of sleep. A blocked nose that “goes away on its own.” Dust that settles again the next day. One by one, we have filed them under “everyone experiences this.” The data from the 2026 Romanian Homes Air Barometer show, however, that Romanians start from the exact opposite premise: they regard their homes as safe spaces. The heart of the problem is not optimism itself, but the contrast between that optimism and what those same people feel at home every day. This contrast is not accidental: according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), indoor air can be up to five times more polluted than outdoor air, while in new or recently renovated homes, emissions from materials and furniture can raise chemical pollutant levels to up to 100 times outdoor levels. Read more about AD/01 has exceeded the threshold of 300 technology professionals in Romania read more We feel the effects, but no longer attribute them to the air Concern does not follow physical experience. Of those who personally experience symptoms – allergies, restless sleep and fatigue – 38% are nevertheless not concerned about the air quality in their homes, and 86% believe their indoor air is as good as or better than the air outside. The explanation, the study shows, is again normalization : chronic fatigue, restless sleep and seasonal allergies come to be treated as natural parts of daily life rather than as possible warning signs coming from one’s own home. The symptom is felt, but it is not attributed to the air. This is not an attitude problem, but an information problem. The pattern is even more visible among the younger generation: of the Gen Z respondents who report problems at home, 74% report personal symptoms such as allergies or respiratory problems, difficulty falling asleep or restless sleep, frequent fatigue or lack of energy – 16 percentage points above the sample average. The difference may reflect both genuinely greater sensitivity and a greater willingness to talk about these symptoms, rather than necessarily poorer air quality. “Air is one of the few elements essential to our health that we have not learned to assess. We pay attention to the water we drink and the food we eat, and we check the temperature in our homes, yet we assume the air quality is good even when we experience symptoms and obvious discomfort. The Ecovent study shows that Romania’s air-quality problem is not a lack of concern for health, but a lack of information. Through this study, we want to help Romanians become more aware of the importance of indoor air quality.” Andrei Agafița, Founder & CEO, Ecovent What we see at home but consider normal The most common problem reported by Romanians is dust that quickly settles on furniture (51%) – usually blamed on cleaning, although rapid dust accumulation is in fact an indicator of poor air circulation. The most widespread technical misconception identified by the study is the confusion between air conditioning and ventilation: 30% of Romanians consider air conditioning a way to improve air quality , although it merely recirculates the air in the room without bringing in fresh outdoor air. In Bucharest-Ilfov, the figure rises to 55%. When reclassified according to their actual impact, the data show that half of households – 50% – use no solution with a real effect on air quality, while 17% stop at cosmetic solutions such as plants, air fresheners and scented candles. This is not a wrong choice, but one unsupported by information: 53% of Romanians do not actually know what a heat-recovery ventilation system is – either they are hearing about it for the first time or they recognize only the term. What the specialist says “Good air quality is essential for optimal long-term health. Although most of us spend much of our time at home, we tend to look for the causes of respiratory conditions exclusively outside it. It is crucial to understand that prolonged exposure to allergens and chemical particles in enclosed spaces causes structural changes in the airways. Over time, these changes lead to chronic lung diseases such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or lung cancer, as well as a poorer quality of life and years lived with illness. It is time to understand this reality and for each of us to take the necessary steps to make the air in our own homes an ally of our health,” says Associate Professor Dr Beatrice Mahler, pulmonologist. On Clean Air Day, from awareness to measurement On the International Day of Clean Air, Ecovent is moving from questions to concrete answers. To help Romanians discover the actual air quality in their own homes, Ecovent is launching the Air Barometer and giving away 1,000 thermohygrometers to monitor indoor temperature and humidity. This effort is designed to make the market more aware of indoor air quality – the first and simplest step toward making monitoring a habit. Registration is available through a dedicated form at https://aercurat.ecovent.ro , and recipients of the device are invited to submit their measurement results. In this way, the project moves from the question, “How clean do Romanians think the air in their homes is?” to “What do measurements in their own homes actually show?” Temperature and humidity are among the easiest values to monitor at home: the optimal humidity range is 40-60%. Below this range, irritation of the airways and skin can occur; above it, the risk of condensation and mould increases. The difference between suspecting and knowing can begin with this simple step. About the methodology The 2026 Romanian Homes Air Barometer is a quantitative usage-and-attitudes study conducted by MKOR Consulting at Ecovent’s initiative, based on a sample of 1,000 respondents in Romania aged 18 to 55. The sample was weighted by gender, age and geographical distribution, in line with the latest data from Romania’s National Institute of Statistics (INS). Data were collected online using the CAWI method between May and June 2026 through the MKOR Panel. The margin of error is ±3.1% at a 95% confidence level. The study measures reported perceptions and behaviours, not physical air-quality values: no measurements of carbon dioxide, humidity or particulate matter were taken. The international reference on indoor pollution comes from EPA studies and describes the general situation, not the homes analysed in this study. Founded in 2017, Ecovent is a Romanian group specializing exclusively in indoor air-quality solutions for residential, commercial and industrial spaces. Ecovent’s portfolio brings together equipment from 30 international brands, as well as products developed under its own Evoair brand, covering heat-recovery ventilation, air purification, humidification and dehumidification solutions.
